--- title: "07 — The compiled LIGO twin (RTSfreerun)" description: "The same P&S pipeline on the real compiled-CDS suspension front-end — open-loop under twin seismic+readout noise, then the 6-DOF plant with the production damping loops closed." image: thumbnails/07.svg categories: [twin, closed-loop, MIMO] freeze: true --- Examples [01–06](index.qmd) identify *teaching* plants — lumped resonances and a coupled normal-mode expansion. This one identifies the **real thing**: a compiled [`rtsfreerun`](https://controlsystems.docs.ligo.org/rtsfreerun) advligorts front-end model of a LIGO HSTS suspension — *the same C filter numerics a control-room front-end runs*, driven through the same channel API, under the digital twin's own seismic and readout noise. No hardware; no method changes. The Pintelon–Schoukens loop (periodic multisine → leakage-free reference FRF → maximum-likelihood fit → Cramér–Rao refinement) runs exactly as it does on the teaching plants. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## What makes this page different The plant here is **not** a Python lumped model — it is the compiled `x1hsts` / `x1hsts6dof` CDS composite (built from a `.mdl` by `rtsfreerun`), carrying the as-built `HSTS_DRV_TF` foton cascade and a 36-state MIMO suspension state space. Because that model is not installed in CI, this page is rendered with `freeze: true` from a locally executed cache; the figures below are real recovery runs against the compiled model, scored against an **analytic oracle** derived from the twin's own filter definitions (`backends.rtsfreerun_oracle`). ::: ::: {#a7ee36b8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue (runs the real models)"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "rtsfreerun_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "rtsfreerun_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np import rtsfreerun_demo as rd ``` ::: ## A1–A2 · Open-loop SISO under the twin's own noise The HSTS drive→sensor plant is the order-10 `HSTS_DRV_TF` cascade — **five modes** near 0.67, 1.01, 1.52, 2.81 and 3.78 Hz, each $Q\!\approx\!50$, threaded with near-cancelling zeros. We inject the multisine at the coil-driver excitation port and read the 16-bit sensor displacement while the twin runs `ligo-india` seismic on the ISI and BOSEM readout noise. The FRF input is the **after-actuator drive monitor**, so the coil driver divides out and the recovered transfer is the bare suspension. *(A1 — the wiring/oracle smoke test that gates this page — lives in the test suite; here we go straight to recovery.)* ### What you'd watch in the control room — one raw measurement Before any fitting, here is the raw audit: a single broadband measurement, exactly the channels you would trend at the front end. The drive is injected through a **3 s Tukey on/off ramp** (actuator-safe — you never slam a suspension), held at full amplitude through the measured periods, then ramped back down; the readout is the real 16-bit sensor under the twin's seismic + BOSEM noise. Nothing here is fitted — it is what went in and what came out. ::: {#5c2ba5db .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="One raw open-loop measurement (Tukey-ramped broadband drive, twin noise)"} a2a = rd.a2_audit(seed=1) rd.drive_response_fig(a2a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: You can see the drive ramp up over 3 s, the suspension ring up to steady state, and the readout carry the modes plus the broadband sensor/seismic floor. The measurement uses only the flat middle periods (the leakage-free, integer-period window), so the ramps fall in discarded settle. ::: {#01836e56 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Excitation design — the flat audit drive vs the point-optimal ASD"} rd.exc_design_fig(a2a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The audit drives **flat** in-band (every line illuminated, so coherence is interpretable everywhere); the campaign below instead spends its power budget where the Fisher information is — the gold ASD concentrates at the five modes. Now the leakage-free reference FRF and its **per-line coherence** — where on the band do we actually trust this measurement? ::: {#6af98cc1 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Measured FRF vs oracle, with per-line coherence"} rd.bode_audit_fig(a2a, fit=a2a.fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Coherence sits at ~1 across the driven band (deterministic drive, modest noise); the measured FRF (markers, with σ error bars) lands on the analytic oracle, and a quick ML fit threads it. The **residuals** — normalised `(measured − fit)/σ` — should be a structureless ±2 scatter with a standard-normal histogram if the noise model is right: ::: {#6372b2e7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Normalised FRF residuals — should be ~N(0,1)"} rd.residuals_fig(a2a, a2a.fit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Optimal-excitation campaign The audit above is a single flat sweep. The actual identification is the P&S **optimal-excitation campaign**: a prior-robust first pass, then point-optimal refinement that concentrates the drive where the Fisher information is, folding each pass in by inverse-variance and refitting. ::: {#07c098b4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Run the A2 optimal-excitation campaign against compiled x1hsts"} a2 = rd.a2_recovery(seed=1, n_passes=3) rd.bode_overlay(a2.ff, a2.oracle, a2.fit, freq=a2.freq, H_meas=a2.H_meas, title="x1hsts drive→sensor — analytic oracle vs P&S recovery (noise on)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The recovered model tracks the oracle through every mode and anti-resonance, and the parameter uncertainty falls pass over pass while the peak drive stays well under the coil-driver limit. ::: {#20ed6b31 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Modal recovery + uncertainty convergence"} display(rd.modes_table(a2.oracle, a2.fit)) rd.convergence_fig(a2.fracs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **HSTS drive→sensor modes — analytic vs recovered** | oracle f₀ [Hz] | recovered f₀ | Δf₀ | oracle Q | recovered Q | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.672 | 0.673 | 0.01% | 50 | 50 | | 1.005 | 1.005 | 0.02% | 50 | 48 | | 1.516 | 1.516 | 0.00% | 50 | 50 | | 2.807 | 2.807 | 0.00% | 50 | 50 | | 3.781 | 3.788 | 0.18% | 50 | 50 | ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## A3 · Closed-loop — the real damping loops engaged Now the `x1hsts6dof` composite: the bare-M1 **6×6 MIMO** HSTS state space with the **production L1 `MC2_M1_DAMP` foton banks** closed around all six rigid-body DOFs (L, T, V, R, P, Y), tuned to a $\tau\!\approx\!5$ s ringdown — the very loops that damp the suspension in the observatory. A closed loop normally *hides* the plant: the sensor sees the suppressed response $G/(1+GC)$, not $G$. The P&S **reference-based** estimate recovers $G$ anyway, by taking the FRF against the **true plant input** — the drive *minus* the controller feedback at the `COIL_DRV_SUM` junction. The feedback sign is load-bearing: negligible off-resonance, it dominates exactly at the damped modes. ::: {#7e648d47 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Drive each DOF open- and closed-loop; recover the plant tensor"} d = rd.a34(n_passes=2) display(rd.diag_table(d)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Median |FRF| error vs the state-space oracle, diagonal elements** | DoF | A4 open-loop | A3 closed-loop | | --- | --- | --- | | L | 0.216% | 0.149% | | T | 0.241% | 0.107% | | V | 0.344% | 0.074% | | R | 0.022% | 0.084% | | P | 0.020% | 0.060% | | Y | 0.037% | 0.027% | ::: ::: With the loops closed, every diagonal element comes back as the **open-loop** plant to a part in a thousand — the controller is cancelled, not fit. That is the whole point of a reference-based closed-loop identification: you measure the suspension you want to model, not the suppressed loop you happened to be running. #### What the cancellation looks like in the raw time series To see *why* it works, here is one raw closed-loop measurement on the L DoF — the four channels a control-room audit would log: the injected `DRIVE_EXC`, the **damper feedback** it provokes, the **reconstructed plant input** (drive − feedback, the `"+-"` `COIL_DRV_SUM` node), and the sensor readout — all with the loops live. ::: {#908aa108 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="One raw closed-loop measurement — drive, damper feedback, plant input, readout"} a3a = rd.a3_audit(d, "L") rd.loop_timeseries_fig(a3a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The damper output is non-trivial (the loop is genuinely active), and the plant input is the drive *minus* it. Taking the FRF against that reconstructed plant input — not the injected drive — cancels the controller and returns the open-loop plant, with coherence at unity: ::: {#fe0b758d .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Closed-loop reference FRF vs the OPEN-loop oracle, with coherence"} rd.bode_audit_fig(a3a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: That table is the *breadth* result — all six loops cancelled at once, nonparametrically. The *depth* result is the **same parametric campaign as [A2](#a1a2-open-loop-siso-under-the-twins-own-noise)**, now run through a closed loop. Taking the longitudinal (L) DoF: we seed an analytic modal prior (its order chosen from the state-space oracle — L carries five modes; pitch and yaw carry fewer, and over-modelling them is what used to break the optimal-excitation design), then run the prior-robust → point-optimal refinement against the reconstructed plant input. ::: {#c568ca83 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="A3 depth — the optimal-excitation parametric campaign, loops closed (L DoF)"} a3 = rd.a3_parametric(d, "L", n_passes=4) rd.bode_overlay(a3.ff, a3.oracle, a3.fit, freq=a3.freq, H_meas=a3.H_meas, title="L drive→sense — open-loop oracle vs closed-loop parametric recovery") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The recovered model sits on the **open-loop** state-space oracle through all five modes — even though the L damper (and the other five) are live. The modal parameters return to the analytic truth, and the Cramér–Rao uncertainty falls pass over pass exactly as in the open-loop case: a closed loop costs nothing here, because the reference-based estimate never saw it. ::: {#7beaa529 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Closed-loop modal recovery + CRB convergence (L DoF)"} display(rd.modes_table(a3.oracle_modes, a3.fit, caption="L-DoF modes — open-loop oracle vs closed-loop recovery")) rd.convergence_fig(a3.fracs) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **L-DoF modes — open-loop oracle vs closed-loop recovery** | oracle f₀ [Hz] | recovered f₀ | Δf₀ | oracle Q | recovered Q | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.672 | 0.672 | 0.07% | 50 | 42 | | 1.005 | 1.019 | 1.37% | 50 | 16 | | 1.516 | 1.516 | 0.06% | 50 | 48 | | 2.807 | 2.807 | 0.00% | 50 | 50 | | 3.782 | 3.983 | 5.33% | 50 | 8 | ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## A4 · The full 6×6 MIMO tensor Opening the loops and driving each input DOF in turn gives the complete drive→sense FRF tensor. The diagonals carry the suspension's anti-resonance notches; the off-diagonals are the genuine cross-coupling — strongest on the L↔P and R↔Y pairs the suspension's geometry dictates. Each per-pair FRF is overlaid on its analytic state-space element below (black line), with the closed-loop diagonal recovery from A3 in green on the diagonal. ::: {#4dd81581 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="6×6 |FRF| tensor — oracle vs open-loop (A4) and closed-loop diagonal (A3)"} rd.tensor_grid(d) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The off-diagonal elements *under closed loop* still carry the cross-loop bias — recovering the coupled matrix jointly, with shared modal poles across elements, is the parametric MIMO fit (the named Track B follow-on). The per-pair open-loop tensor here is the honest nonparametric MIMO result, and the closed-loop diagonal is the controller-cancelled SISO recovery — both against the same compiled twin a real front-end runs.
